docs.title: gpuprov
docs.text:
A mini-SkyPilot in Rust. gpuprov provisions a GPU VM on the cheapest cloud offer that has capacity, waits until you can SSH in, and records it locally. Optionally it turns the VM into a single-node k3s cluster, so you can deploy containers with plain kubectl.

$ gpuprov provision --name dev --gpus L4:1 --cloud gcp --region us-central1 --region us-east1
[dev] planning on gcp
[dev] preparing g2-standard-4@us-central1/us-central1-a
[dev] creating g2-standard-4@us-central1/us-central1-a
[dev] tearing down at us-central1/us-central1-a (Requesting) then next offer   # ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED
[dev] preparing g2-standard-4@us-central1/us-central1-b
...
VM 'dev' is UP
  Endpoint:    ubuntu@34.122.x.x:22
  Connect:     gpuprov ssh dev    (or plain: ssh dev)

$ gpuprov ssh dev -- nvidia-smi
$ gpuprov down dev

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Multi-cloud, one interface. AWS (EC2), GCP (Compute Engine), Prime Intellect (a GPU marketplace), and a local Docker "cloud" for tests all sit behind one CloudProvider trait of six idempotent primitives.
  • Failover that does not leak. Offers are tried in price order. A capacity error tears down the partial attempt and moves on, and a quota error skips the whole region. If teardown cannot be confirmed, the VM is recorded as LEAKED instead of being forgotten.
  • Durable state machines. Every operation is journaled in local SQLite. Ctrl-C cleans up what the run created, and a crash resumes from the last state. It never creates a second instance, because every step observes the cloud before it acts. See State machines.
  • SSH-native. One local ed25519 key and a per-VM ~/.ssh/config entry, so plain ssh dev, VS Code Remote, and rsync work.
  • Kubernetes when you want it. --k8s installs k3s over SSH, wires up the NVIDIA device plugin on GPU nodes, validates the cluster, and writes a kubeconfig. It uses a direct API endpoint on clouds that can open ports and an SSH tunnel on clouds that can't.
  • No server. A single static binary with state in ~/.gpu-provisioner.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From crates.ioFrom source 
cargo install gpu-provisioner      # installs the `gpuprov` binary

git clone https://github.com/DumbAI/gpu-provisioner
cd gpu-provisioner
cargo install --path .

Requirements: Rust 1.91.1 or newer, and the system OpenSSH client (ssh) on your PATH. On macOS and Linux it is already there.

docs.title: Try it without a cloud account
docs.text:
The docker cloud runs each "VM" as a local sshd container. It's the quickest way to see the whole lifecycle:

gpuprov provision --cloud docker --name demo --instance-type container
gpuprov ssh demo -- uname -a
gpuprov status demo        # the journaled state transitions
gpuprov down demo

docs.title: Your first cloud VM
docs.text:
1. Credentials. Use whatever each cloud's own tooling already uses. Details are in Configuration.

    • AWS: aws configure (or a profile in ~/.gpu-provisioner/config.toml).
    • GCP: gcloud auth login and gcloud config set project <id>.
    • Prime Intellect: prime login, or PRIME_API_KEY.

  2. Provision.

    # AWS: the cheapest T4 type in us-west-2, falling back to us-east-1
gpuprov provision --name dev --gpus T4:1 --region us-west-2 --region us-east-1

# GCP: an L4 in any zone of us-central1
gpuprov provision --cloud gcp --name dev-gcp --gpus L4:1 --region us-central1

# Prime Intellect: the cheapest H100 offer anywhere in the marketplace
gpuprov provision --cloud primeintellect --name dev-pi --gpus H100:1

    The command blocks until SSH works. Progress goes to stderr and the summary to stdout.

  3. Use it.

    gpuprov ssh dev                    # interactive shell
gpuprov ssh dev -- nvidia-smi      # one command; the exit code propagates
ssh dev                            # plain OpenSSH works too
gpuprov list

  4. Tear it down. VMs bill until you do.

    gpuprov down dev

docs.title: When things go wrong
docs.text:
• Ctrl-C during provision finishes the in-flight cloud call, then deletes what this run created. Press it twice to exit immediately. Re-running the same command then resumes from the journal.
  • gpuprov status <name> shows the last operation and its recent transitions, including why each failed offer was skipped.
  • A VM shown as LEAKED means teardown could not be confirmed. Run gpuprov down <name> again, or gpuprov provision with the same name, which cleans up first.

docs.title: Adding a cloud
docs.text:
A cloud is one module under src/provider/<id>/ that implements CloudProvider, plus one line in provider::build. Nothing above the trait changes. Failover, retries, polling, deadlines, compensation, crash recovery, the journal, SSH, and k3s all come from the shared core.

#[async_trait]
pub trait CloudProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;                 // "mycloud": recorded on every VM row
    fn capabilities(&self) -> Capabilities;         // unsupported features + timing hints
    async fn plan(&self, req: &ResourceRequest) -> Result<Vec<Offer>, ProviderError>;
    async fn prepare(&self, offer: &Offer, spec: &InstanceSpec) -> Result<serde_json::Value, ProviderError>;
    async fn create(&self, offer: &Offer, prepared: &serde_json::Value, spec: &InstanceSpec) -> Result<String, ProviderError>;
    async fn observe(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<Vec<Observed>, ProviderError>;
    async fn delete(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str, ids: &[String]) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
    async fn cleanup(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
}

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Primitive Must Must not plan return offers in preference order (cheapest first). Put anything create needs (marketplace ids, sockets) into Offer::detail. create anything prepare be idempotent per (VM, location): firewall/security group, key registration, image resolution. Return private JSON; it is journaled. create the instance create make one attempt and label everything with the VM identity (tag, label, or name gpuprov-<vm>) wait for running, or retry observe return all non-terminated instances with that identity, with normalized InstanceStatus, and the SshEndpoint once reachable (user/port if the cloud dictates them) filter out broken instances (report them as Failed) delete request deletion; unknown or already-gone ids count as success wait cleanup delete per-VM side resources; idempotent touch shared resources (keys, VPCs)

Long waits belong to the core, which polls observe using your Capabilities { boot_timeout, delete_timeout, poll_interval }. The one exception is a bounded wait on a cloud operation whose result carries the error, as with GCP's operations.wait after instances.insert.

docs.title: Classifying errors
docs.text:
Map every API failure to an ErrorKind. This is the entire failover policy, and it lives in your error.rs:

Kind Use for Core does Transient throttling, 5xx, timeouts retries the step with backoff. Creating observes first, so a request that actually landed is adopted, not duplicated. Capacity stockouts tears down, blocks the offer, and moves to the next Quota account limits tears down and blocks the whole region (override with with_block) Unavailable not viable here and nothing was created blocks the offer with no teardown Failed anything else after resources may exist tears down, blocks the offer, and moves to the next InvalidRequest the ask can't be satisfied (unknown GPU, bad zone) aborts Credentials auth failures tears down what may exist, then aborts

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. src/provider/<id>/mod.rs, with pub const PROVIDER_ID, the provider struct, and the trait impl. Cite the SkyPilot analog in the module doc if one exists.
  2. A config section in config.rs, and an arm in AppConfig::default_regions if your region names differ from AWS's.
  3. Register it in provider::build and PROVIDER_IDS.
  4. Tests: pure tests for parsing and classification, plus wiremock tests for every HTTP primitive. Add a test-only constructor that takes a base URL so tests never read env or credential files. See provider/primeintellect and provider/gcp.
  5. A page under docs/clouds/, and a row in the comparison table.

docs.title: Provisioning State Machines — Design
docs.text: Status: implemented. This page describes the code in src/machine/, src/vm/, src/cluster/, and src/provider/. Section 1 records the review of the previous design that motivated it. Scope: the VM lifecycle state machine (launch, teardown), the k3s cluster state machine layered on it, and the provider contract that AWS, Prime Intellect, GCP and the Docker test cloud implement.

docs.title: 1. Review of the previous design
docs.text:
The previous pipeline (orchestrator.rs → failover.rs → CloudProvider) was a faithful, readable port of SkyPilot's provision_with_retries, with a sound error taxonomy. Its weaknesses showed up as soon as a second, differently-shaped cloud (Prime Intellect) was attempted:

# Problem Where Consequence 1 The state machine is implicit. The DB stored PROVISIONING/UP/FAILED/TERMINATED; the real stages (plan, bootstrap, create, wait-running, wait-ssh, persist, k3s) existed only as control flow. orchestrator::launch, failover::provision_with_failover A crash or Ctrl-C mid-launch lost the failover cursor and any created instance id. Recovery depended on name-tag find-or-create in the one region still on the row. 2 Leak paths. TeardownFailed marked the row FAILED and moved on. FAILED/PROVISIONING rows were never reconciled. A fatal error (e.g. credentials) after create aborted with no teardown. failover.rs, orchestrator.rs:76 Billing resources could outlive every record pointing at them. 3 Coarse, loop-heavy provider trait. provision = bootstrap + find-or-create; wait_running polled for up to 10 minutes inside the adapter, and the engine retried it 3× (up to 30 min). Retry/backoff/polling was re-implemented per adapter. provider/aws/instance.rs:34, failover.rs:24 Every new cloud re-wrote the robustness logic, which is where bugs hide. 4 AWS-shaped assumptions above the trait. The SSH endpoint was public_ip:22 with a client-chosen user; the key travelled by cloud-init; ports, AMI and spot were assumed. orchestrator::finalize, ssh/config_file.rs Marketplace clouds (Prime Intellect: provider-chosen user and NAT port, keys registered via API, no firewall API) did not fit. 5 Blocklist scope fixed at (type, region). failover.rs:139 Quota errors (region-wide) retried every type. Marketplace offers (one per data center) were over-blocked. 6 k3s lived in main.rs, outside any state. finalize_kubernetes ran after the VM was marked UP. The installer travelled by cloud-init and readiness was kubectl get nodes on the node. main.rs:194, kube.rs A failed k3s install left an UP VM with no record of it. k3s only worked on clouds with cloud-init and inbound ports. A closed port 6443 was not caught.

docs.title: 2. Goals
docs.text:
1. One shared, failure-tolerant core. Retries, backoff, polling, deadlines, cancellation, crash-resume and compensation (teardown) are written once.
  2. Thin, uniform cloud adapters. An adapter exposes small, idempotent primitives and classifies its errors; it contains no loops or sleeps beyond a single API call's own pagination.
  3. No silent leaks. Every state that may own a cloud resource knows where it is. A failed teardown is a persistent Leaked state that the next command must resolve.
  4. Composable machines. The k3s machine embeds the VM machine as a child and adds its own durable steps.
  5. Stay true to the PRD wedge: a single binary with local SQLite state and no server.

docs.title: 3. Alternatives considered
docs.text: Decision Options Choice and rationale Execution model (a) implicit control flow (status quo) · (b) edge-triggered workflow of explicit persisted states · (c) level-triggered reconciler (Kubernetes-controller style: desired vs observed, loop until converged) · (d) external durable-execution engine (Temporal) (b) with (c) inside each step. Failover is an ordered search with a cursor, which is naturally a workflow. But each step is written as observe → act if needed → observe (e.g. Creating first looks for an existing instance before calling create), so re-running any step after a crash is safe. (d) violates the single-binary constraint. State encoding Rust typestate · hand-rolled enum + step() · FSM crate (statig, rust-fsm) enum + step(). Typestate cannot be serialized and resumed after a crash. A crate adds a dependency but still needs custom persistence. Serde enums give persistence for free. Provider granularity Coarse (provision, wait) · fine primitives (plan / prepare / create / observe / delete / cleanup) Fine primitives. Coarse calls let an adapter optimise, but they duplicate polling and retry and hide progress from the journal. Fine primitives move all waiting into the core. Passing offer details from plan to launch Encode in the instance-type string (SkyPilot PI: a__b__c__d) · adapter-side cache · opaque detail JSON on the Offer, persisted Persisted JSON survives crashes, keeps the core cloud-agnostic, and avoids string parsing. Transient-error retries Per adapter · central (core) One retry policy and one budget. Adapters return ErrorKind::Transient. SDK-internal retries for reads stay, since they are cheap and safe. k3s installer delivery cloud-init at boot · push over SSH after Ready SSH push works on every cloud (Prime Intellect has no cloud-init), is observable and retryable as its own state, and works on reused VMs. Cost: the install runs after SSH is up instead of during boot, roughly 1–2 minutes slower. k3s API access Always public :6443 · Direct when the cloud can open ports, else SshTunnel Makes k3s portable to clouds without a firewall API. Validation checks the access path the user will actually use. Projection vs source of truth One table · machines (journal, source of truth) + vms (user-facing projection) The generic executor must not know VM columns. vms is updated idempotently by steps and can always be recomputed.

docs.title: 4. Architecture
docs.text:
main.rs ─ CLI: provision / down / status / ssh / kubeconfig / tunnel / list
  cluster/k3s.rs      K3sMachine     = Vm(child LaunchMachine) → Install → ApiReady → Kubeconfig → Validate
  vm/launch.rs        LaunchMachine  = Reconcile → Plan → [Prepare → Create → Boot → Connect]* → Ready
  vm/teardown.rs      TeardownMachine= Request → AwaitGone → Cleanup → Done   (also the compensation sub-machine)
    machine/          Executor<M: Machine>: persist · retry budget · backoff · poll · deadline · cancel · resume
                      Journal (SQLite `machines` + `machine_events`)
      provider/mod.rs CloudProvider: capabilities · plan · prepare · create · observe · delete · cleanup
        provider/{aws, primeintellect, gcp, docker}/   — the only code that talks to a cloud API

docs.title: 4.1 The provider contract (provider/mod.rs)
docs.text:
#[async_trait]
pub trait CloudProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn capabilities(&self) -> Capabilities;                       // unsupported features, boot timeout, poll interval
    async fn plan(&self, req: &ResourceRequest) -> Result<Vec<Offer>, ProviderError>;
    async fn prepare(&self, offer: &Offer, spec: &InstanceSpec) -> Result<serde_json::Value, ProviderError>;
    async fn create(&self, offer: &Offer, prepared: &serde_json::Value, spec: &InstanceSpec)
        -> Result<String /* instance id */, ProviderError>;
    async fn observe(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<Vec<Observed>, ProviderError>;
    async fn delete(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str, instance_ids: &[String]) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
    async fn cleanup(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
}

Semantics every adapter must honour. These are checked by the shared conformance tests and the fake-provider tests.

Primitive Contract plan Ordered offers (preference = order). Pure catalog/availability lookup that creates nothing. Unplannable ask → InvalidRequest. prepare Idempotent per-(VM, location) prerequisites (security group, firewall rule, SSH-key registration, image resolution). Returns driver-private JSON, persisted. create One creation attempt. Every resource is labelled with the VM identity (gpuprov-vm-name=<name> tag or label, or the gpuprov-<name> name). No waiting for running. observe All non-terminated instances carrying the identity at that location, with normalised status and the SSH endpoint once known. delete Request deletion of the given instances. Idempotent: an unknown or already-deleted instance is success. Does not wait. cleanup Delete per-VM side resources after instances are gone. Idempotent.

Normalised status: Pending | Running | Stopping | Stopped | Terminating | Failed(reason). The core treats an instance as booted when it is Running and reports an SshEndpoint { host, port, user? }. That covers the AWS public-IP lag and Prime Intellect's late sshConnection.

ProviderError { kind, msg, block } drives the core:

ErrorKind Core action Default block scope Transient retry the same step with backoff (budgeted) — Capacity compensate → block → next offer the offer Quota compensate → block → next offer the whole region (all types) Unavailable block → next offer, no compensation (nothing created) the offer Failed compensate → block → next offer the offer InvalidRequest, Credentials compensate if something may exist → Aborted —

An adapter may override the scope through block (for example AWS Unsupported → instance type in region).

docs.title: 4.2 The executor (machine/)
docs.text:
#[async_trait]
pub trait Machine: Send + Sync {
    type State: Serialize + DeserializeOwned + Clone + Debug + Send + Sync;
    const KIND: &'static str;
    fn is_terminal(&self, s: &Self::State) -> bool;
    fn label(&self, s: &Self::State) -> String;                       // journal / progress line
    async fn step(&self, s: &Self::State, cx: &StepCx) -> Step<Self::State>;
    fn retry_policy(&self, s: &Self::State) -> RetryPolicy { RetryPolicy::default() }
    fn on_retries_exhausted(&self, s: &Self::State, last_error: String) -> Self::State;
    fn on_cancel(&self, s: &Self::State) -> Option<Self::State> { None }
}

pub enum Step<S> {
    Next(S),                                   // transition, persisted before the next step runs
    Poll { after: Duration, note: String },   // not done yet: same state, no budget consumed
    Retry { error: String },                  // transient: same state, backoff, budget consumed
}

Executor invariants:

  1. Write-ahead. A transition is journalled before the next step's side effect. Steps that produce a handle (for example Creating → Booting { instance_id }) return it in the next state, so it is durable before any wait begins.
  2. Idempotent steps. Because a crash can happen after a side effect but before its transition is journalled, each step tolerates re-execution (observe first).
  3. Budgets. Consecutive Retrys in one state are capped (RetryPolicy { max_attempts, initial_backoff, max_backoff }). On exhaustion the machine names the failure state; the executor never invents one. Poll deadlines are enforced by the machine using cx.in_state (time since entering the state in this process), so a resume gets a fresh but bounded window.
  4. Cancellation at step boundaries only. Ctrl-C never drops an in-flight cloud call (that would lose the handle). Between steps, on_cancel maps the state to a compensating state (for example Booting → Compensating). The machine then runs to a terminal state, and a second Ctrl-C exits immediately and leaves the journal resumable.
  5. Resume. Executor::run loads the journalled state for the key. If it is non-terminal, execution continues from it; otherwise the caller supplies a fresh initial state.

docs.title: 4.3 VM launch machine (vm/launch.rs)
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Reconciling
    Reconciling --> Connecting: UP record & cloud says Running (reuse)
    Reconciling --> Compensating: journal shows Leaked / stale attempt
    Reconciling --> Planning
    Planning --> Preparing: offers (cursor = 0)
    Planning --> Aborted: InvalidRequest / Credentials
    Preparing --> Creating
    Creating --> Booting: instance id (or adopted existing)
    Booting --> Connecting: Running + SSH endpoint
    Connecting --> Ready: SSH login OK, ssh config + vms row written
    Preparing --> NextOffer: Unavailable (no compensation)
    Creating --> Compensating: Capacity / Quota / Failed
    Booting --> Compensating: Failed status / boot timeout / vanished
    Connecting --> Compensating: SSH timeout
    Compensating --> NextOffer: teardown complete → block scope
    Compensating --> Leaked: teardown exhausted
    NextOffer --> Preparing: next unblocked offer
    NextOffer --> Exhausted: none left
    Exhausted --> Planning: --retry-until-up (after 30 s)
    Ready --> [*]
    Aborted --> [*]
    Leaked --> [*]

Search { offers, cursor, blocked, history } travels in every attempt state, so the failover cursor survives a crash. Leaked { location, instance_ids, reason } is terminal for this run, but the next provision or down for the name starts by compensating it, and list/status show it.

docs.title: 4.4 Teardown machine (vm/teardown.rs)
docs.text: Requesting → AwaitingGone → CleaningUp → Done | Leaked. It is used standalone by down and embedded by the launch machine's Compensating state, so one teardown implementation serves both paths.

docs.title: 4.5 k3s cluster machine (cluster/k3s.rs)
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Vm
    Vm --> Installing: child LaunchMachine Ready
    Vm --> Failed: child Exhausted / Aborted / Leaked
    Installing --> AwaitingApi: installer pushed over SSH (idempotent)
    AwaitingApi --> FetchingKubeconfig: /readyz ok
    FetchingKubeconfig --> Validating: kubeconfig written (Direct or SshTunnel)
    Validating --> Ready: node Ready, CoreDNS up, GPU allocatable (GPU nodes), API reachable via access path
    Installing --> Failed: retries exhausted
    AwaitingApi --> Failed: timeout
    Validating --> Failed: timeout
    Ready --> [*]
    Failed --> [*]
  • Composition. K3sState::Vm(LaunchState) delegates step to the child machine and lifts its result. A child terminal Ready(vm) becomes Installing { vm }. One journal row per VM name holds the whole nested state.
  • Access mode. Direct (the cloud opens 6443/80/443) or SshTunnel (gpuprov tunnel <name> forwards 127.0.0.1:6443). The choice comes from provider capabilities, so k3s works on Prime Intellect.
  • Failure policy. k3s failures leave the VM up (Failed { vm }) for debugging. gpuprov down removes it, and gpuprov provision --k8s re-enters at Installing.

docs.title: 5. Adapters
docs.text: Primitive AWS (EC2) Prime Intellect (REST) GCP (Compute REST) Docker (test cloud) plan static GPU→type ladder × regions live GET /availability/gpus → one offer per data center, cheapest first static GPU→machine-type ladder × zones that offer the type (live) one offer, local prepare type metadata, zones offering it, AMI, default-VPC subnets, per-VM SG find-or-register SSH key → sshKeyId; re-validate offer per-VM firewall rule (network tag); image family → image build the sshd image if missing create RunInstances (fail-fast client, subnets in order) POST /pods with offer's cloudId/socket/dc + sshKeyId instances.insert + wait for the zone operation docker run sshd with authorized_keys observe DescribeInstances by tag GET /pods by name, sshConnection → user/port instances.list by label docker ps/inspect by label, mapped port delete TerminateInstances DELETE /pods/{id} instances.delete docker rm -f cleanup delete SG — delete firewall rule — unsupported — ports, image, spot — ports, image, spot

docs.title: 6. Testing
docs.text:
• Executor tests: a toy machine checks persistence, resume after a simulated crash, retry exhaustion, and the cancellation mapping.
  • Launch-machine tests: a scripted FakeProvider covers failover across offers, quota blocking a region, crash between create and journal (adopts the instance and does not create a duplicate), fatal error after create (compensates), and a failed teardown (Leaked, resolved by the next run).
  • Adapter tests: pure classification and parsing tests. HTTP adapters (Prime Intellect, GCP) run against wiremock.
  • Integration (tests/docker_e2e.rs, #[ignore] unless Docker is present): the docker provider provisions a real sshd container through the full launch machine, runs a command over SSH, re-provisions idempotently, and tears down. Run with cargo test --test docker_e2e -- --ignored.

docs.title: Clouds
docs.text:
Every cloud is an adapter behind the same six-primitive CloudProvider contract. The shared state machines supply failover, retries, compensation, and crash recovery. The table shows how the clouds differ.

AWS GCP Prime Intellect Docker --cloud aws (default) gcp primeintellect docker What a "VM" is EC2 instance Compute Engine instance marketplace pod local sshd container Region names us-west-2 us-central1 united_states, canada, … local Zone AZ (us-west-2a) zone (us-central1-a) data center id — Empty region list error error anywhere local Catalog static GPU ladder static GPU ladder + live zone offerings live availability API — SSH key delivery cloud-init ssh-keys metadata + cloud-init API (sshKeyId per pod) container env SSH user / port ubuntu / 22 ubuntu / 22 dictated by the pod ubuntu / random local port --port, --k8s direct API ✓ (security group) ✓ (firewall rule) ✗ (k8s uses SSH tunnel) ✗ (VM lifecycle only) --spot ✓ ✓ (SPOT, delete on preemption) ✗ ✗ --image AMI id image URL / family ✗ ✗ Per-VM side resources security group firewall rule — —

Unsupported combinations are rejected before planning, with the cloud's reason. For example, --port 8080 on Prime Intellect is refused because its pods expose SSH only and there is no firewall API.

docs.title: AWS
docs.text: gpuprov provision --name dev --gpus A10G:1 --region us-east-2 --region us-west-2

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
A GPU ask maps to a ladder of EC2 types, cheapest first: same GPU, more CPU and RAM as you go up. The ladder is crossed type-major with your regions, so the cheapest type is tried in every region before a bigger one.

GPU count → types T4 1 → g4dn.xlarge … g4dn.16xlarge · 4 → g4dn.12xlarge · 8 → g4dn.metal A10G 1 → g5.xlarge … g5.16xlarge · 4 → g5.12xlarge, g5.24xlarge · 8 → g5.48xlarge L4 1 → g6.xlarge … g6.16xlarge · 4 → g6.12xlarge, g6.24xlarge · 8 → g6.48xlarge L40S 1 → g6e.xlarge … g6e.16xlarge · 4 → g6e.12xlarge, g6e.24xlarge · 8 → g6e.48xlarge A100 · A100-80GB · H100 · H200 8 → p4d.24xlarge · p4de.24xlarge · p5.48xlarge · p5e.48xlarge

docs.title: Prepare (per offer)
docs.text:
This is a port of SkyPilot's sky/provision/aws/config.py, ordered cheapest check first so a region that isn't viable fails before anything is created:

  1. Instance-type metadata (GPU, architecture) and the zones that actually offer the type.
  2. AMI: the Ubuntu / Deep Learning AMI matching GPU and architecture, resolved through SSM public parameters (or --image). Its root device and minimum disk size are validated.
  3. Public subnets in the default VPC, restricted to the offering zones.
  4. A per-VM security group (gpuprov-<name>) opening 22 plus requested ports.

Default AMIs, keyed on the instance type's live metadata:

x86_64 arm64 CPU Canonical Ubuntu 22.04 Canonical Ubuntu 22.04 (arm64) GPU Deep Learning Base AMI (OSS NVIDIA driver) Deep Learning Base AMI arm64 (OSS NVIDIA driver)

Pre-Turing GPUs (K80/V100/M60) are not supported by the OSS driver; pass --image for those. A --disk smaller than the AMI's snapshot is rejected with the required size.

docs.title: Create / observe / delete
docs.text:
• RunInstances uses a no-retry client and walks the zones' subnets on capacity errors. Instances use IMDSv2 and gp3 root disks, and are tagged gpuprov-vm-name=<name> and gpuprov-managed=true. The SSH key travels in cloud-init; no EC2 key pairs are created.
  • observe uses DescribeInstances filtered by the identity tag. delete is TerminateInstances (a not-found instance counts as success). cleanup deletes the security group, retrying while ENIs detach.

docs.title: Error mapping
docs.text: AWS code Kind Effect InsufficientInstanceCapacity, InsufficientCapacity, … Capacity compensate, next offer VcpuLimitExceeded, InstanceLimitExceeded, MaxSpotInstanceCountExceeded Quota skip the whole region Unsupported Unavailable skip this type in the region RequestLimitExceeded, InternalError, … Transient retry with backoff AuthFailure, ExpiredToken, … Credentials abort (after compensating)

docs.title: IAM permissions
docs.text: The caller needs ec2:Describe*, ec2:RunInstances, ec2:TerminateInstances, ec2:CreateTags, ec2:CreateSecurityGroup, ec2:DeleteSecurityGroup, ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, and ssm:GetParameter (public AMI parameters). The VM itself gets no IAM role.

docs.title: Docker (local test cloud)
docs.text:
The docker cloud runs each "VM" as a long-running sshd container on your local Docker daemon. It exists so the real state machines (journaling, failover bookkeeping, SSH probing, reuse, crash adoption, teardown) can run end to end without a cloud account. CI uses it the same way.

gpuprov provision --cloud docker --name demo --instance-type container
gpuprov ssh demo -- 'whoami && sudo -n true && echo ok'
gpuprov down demo
Primitive Docker plan one offer in region local (GPU asks are rejected) prepare check the daemon; build the embedded sshd image on first use (its tag includes the Dockerfile hash) create docker run -d, labeled gpuprov-vm-name=<name>, SSH published on 127.0.0.1:<random port> observe docker ps -a by label, plus docker inspect for status and mapped port delete docker rm -f

The container's entrypoint gives the same login contract that cloud-init gives a real VM: $SSH_USER with passwordless sudo and the public key authorized.

Containers don't run systemd, so --k8s cannot install k3s here. Use this cloud for VM-lifecycle testing.

docs.title: GCP
docs.text:
gcloud auth login && gcloud config set project my-project
gpuprov provision --cloud gcp --name dev --gpus L4:1 --region us-central1 --region us-east1

The adapter calls the Compute Engine v1 REST API directly. Authentication uses an OAuth access token from [gcp] access_token, $GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN, or gcloud auth print-access-token (cached and refreshed). Leaving out service-account key signing keeps the binary free of crypto dependencies.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
GCP capacity is zonal, so offers are per zone. The GPU ladder below is crossed with the zones of each region, but only zones that actually offer the machine type (live aggregated/machineTypes / aggregated/acceleratorTypes) are kept.

GPU count → machine types T4 1 → n1-standard-4/8/16 · 2 → n1-standard-8/16 · 4 → n1-standard-16/32 (T4 attached as a guest accelerator) L4 1 → g2-standard-4 … g2-standard-32 · 2 → g2-standard-24 · 4 → g2-standard-48 · 8 → g2-standard-96 A100 1/2/4/8 → a2-highgpu-{1,2,4,8}g A100-80GB 1/2/4/8 → a2-ultragpu-{1,2,4,8}g H100 1/2/4/8 → a3-highgpu-{1,2,4,8}g

docs.title: Prepare / create
docs.text:
• prepare makes sure a per-VM firewall rule gpuprov-<name> exists, allowing tcp:22 plus requested ports to the instance's network tag. It also resolves the image: the Deep Learning VM family common-cu129-ubuntu-2204-nvidia-580 for GPU types (CUDA 12.9, driver 580), and ubuntu-2204-lts otherwise, unless you pass --image.
  • create runs instances.insert with labels gpuprov-vm-name/gpuprov-managed, ssh-keys and cloud-init user-data metadata, a public NAT IP, and onHostMaintenance=TERMINATE for GPUs. --spot gives a SPOT instance that is deleted on preemption. It then waits for the zone operation, a bounded wait, because stockouts only show up in the finished operation.

docs.title: Error mapping
docs.text: Operation / HTTP error Kind Effect ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED(_WITH_DETAILS), UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION, RESOURCE_NOT_READY Capacity next zone QUOTA_EXCEEDED (incl. GPUS_ALL_REGIONS) Quota skip the region VPC_NOT_FOUND Unavailable skip the region 429 / 5xx / network Transient retry 401, non-quota 403 Credentials abort

docs.title: Prime Intellect
docs.text:
Prime Intellect is a GPU marketplace. It resells capacity from upstream providers (Hyperstack, Lambda, DataCrunch, Nebius, …) behind one API, which makes it a natural fit for failover across providers.

export PRIME_API_KEY=...          # or `prime login`, or [primeintellect] api_key
gpuprov provision --cloud primeintellect --name dev --gpus H100:1
gpuprov provision --cloud primeintellect --name dev2 --gpus A100:8 --region united_states

docs.title: Planning: live availability
docs.text:
Unlike SkyPilot, which reads a static vms.csv catalog, gpuprov queries GET /api/v1/availability/gpus live. A marketplace's stock changes minute to minute, so a static catalog is stale on arrival. Each in-stock offer becomes one candidate:

  • instance_type = <provider>/<cloudId> (e.g. hyperstack/n3-H100x1)
  • region = a Prime Intellect region id (united_states, canada, eu_west, …). No --region means anywhere.
  • zone = the data center id, which --zone pins
  • ordered by on-demand price, cheapest first

GPU names match on a boundary: H100 matches H100_80GB, A100 matches both A100 sizes, H200 does not match GH200, and A10 does not match A100. --instance-type accepts <provider>/<cloudId> or a bare cloudId.

docs.title: Prepare / create
docs.text:
• prepare looks up or registers our public key under /ssh_keys and passes its id per pod (sshKeyId), leaving the account's primary key alone. It then re-checks stock for that exact offer, so a stale plan fails before anything is created.
  • create posts /pods using the offer's own socket (SkyPilot hard-codes PCIe, which is wrong for SXM offers), data center, security tier, and image. Pods are named gpuprov-<name>.

docs.title: SSH and Kubernetes
docs.text: The SSH user and port come from the pod's sshConnection (often root and a NAT port), not from --ssh-user. Pods expose SSH only, so --port is rejected, and --k8s clusters use SSH-tunnel access.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: These are declared as unsupported features and rejected up front: --port (no firewall API), --image (images come from the offer's environment list), and --spot. Pods can take up to about 16 minutes to become active; the boot timeout matches SkyPilot's.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: gpuprov ships as the gpu-provisioner crate on crates.io; it provides the gpuprov binary and the gpu_provisioner library.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Bump version in Cargo.toml (semver).
  2. Make sure CI is green, and run the e2e suite locally if Docker-touching code changed.

  3. Check what will be uploaded. Cargo.toml include limits the package to src/, tests/, examples/*.yaml, Cargo.lock, the README, and the LICENSE. The docs site and design notes stay out.

    cargo package --list
cargo publish --dry-run

  4. Publish (irreversible: a version can be yanked but never re-used or deleted):

    cargo login            # token from https://crates.io/me
cargo publish
git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme from docs/:

uv run --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs serve        # http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs build --strict
uv run --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs gh-deploy    # publish to GitHub Pages

(Use pip install -r docs/requirements.txt in place of uv if you prefer.)

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
cargo test                       # all unit tests: no cloud or Docker needed
cargo test vm::launch            # one module (substring match)
cargo test quota_blocks_every_type_in_the_region   # one test
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
cargo test --test docker_e2e -- --ignored --nocapture   # end-to-end, needs Docker

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Layer How it's tested Executor (machine/) a toy machine: journaling, retry-budget exhaustion, resume from a journaled state, cancel → compensation, cancel → resumable Launch / teardown / k3s machines provider::fake::FakeProvider, a small simulated cloud with scripted per-offer behaviors (Boots, CreateFails, CreatedButErrors, BootFails, NeverBoots, …), injectable delete failures, a call log, and a max-concurrent-instances counter for leak and duplicate checks Adapters pure parsing and classification tests, plus wiremock HTTP servers for Prime Intellect and GCP End to end tests/docker_e2e.rs: the Docker cloud plus real SSH. It provisions, runs a command, re-provisions (reuse), simulates a crash after create (adopts the container, no duplicate), and tears down.

Async tests run on paused time (#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]), so the machines' 5-second polls and 30-second backoffs cost nothing. Database tests use Db::open_in_memory().

The launch-machine suite pins the behaviors that matter most:

  • capacity triggers compensation and moves to the next region; quota skips the whole region; unavailable skips without teardown
  • a transient create error after the request landed adopts the instance instead of creating a second one
  • a fatal error after create tears down before aborting
  • a failed teardown becomes LEAKED, and the next run cleans up first
  • a crash while Booting resumes without a second create
  • an unsupported feature is rejected even when a running VM could be reused, and the VM's record is left untouched

docs.title: CI
docs.text: Workflow Runs .github/workflows/unit.yml fmt, clippy (-D warnings), unit tests on Linux and macOS, MSRV (1.91.1) check .github/workflows/integration.yml the Docker e2e suite on Linux, with GPUPROV_E2E_REQUIRE_DOCKER=1 so a missing daemon fails the job instead of skipping

docs.title: Manual testing against real clouds
docs.text: Use GPUPROV_HOME=/tmp/gp to keep state away from ~/.gpu-provisioner, and RUST_LOG=debug for verbose progress. gpuprov status <name> shows the journaled transitions with failure details.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
Global flag: --config <PATH> selects the config file (default ~/.gpu-provisioner/config.toml; see Configuration).

Environment: GPUPROV_HOME relocates all local state, and RUST_LOG=debug gives verbose progress. Logs go to stderr and summaries to stdout.

docs.title: gpuprov provision
docs.text:
Provision a VM and block until it is SSH-ready. With --k8s, it also blocks until the cluster is validated. Re-running the command with the same --name is idempotent: a running VM is verified and reused, and an interrupted run is resumed.

Flag Meaning --name <NAME> VM name: lowercase letters, digits and -, up to 40 characters. It also works as name: in the spec file. --spec <FILE> YAML spec file. Flags override its fields. --cloud <ID> aws (default), gcp, primeintellect, or docker. --instance-type <T> Exact type: g5.xlarge, g2-standard-8, hyperstack/n3-H100x1, or container. Cannot be combined with --gpus. --gpus <NAME[:N]> GPU shorthand resolved by the cloud's catalog, e.g. T4:1, L4:1, A100-80GB:8, H100:8. --region <R> Candidate region, in failover order. Repeatable. Region names are cloud-specific. --zone <Z> Pin to one zone (AWS and GCP) or data center (Prime Intellect). --image <ID> (alias --ami) Machine-image override. --disk <GB> Root disk size (default 100). --spot Spot or preemptible capacity, where the cloud supports it. --port <P> Extra inbound port besides SSH. Repeatable. Requires a cloud with firewall control. --ssh-user <U> Login user to create (default ubuntu). Marketplace clouds dictate their own. --k8s Install single-node k3s and write a kubeconfig (guide). --retry-until-up When every offer fails, wait 30s and re-plan, forever.

Unsupported feature/cloud combinations, such as --port on Prime Intellect, are rejected before anything is planned.

Spec file example:

name: trainer
cloud: gcp
gpus: L4:1
regions: [us-central1, us-east1]
disk_gb: 200
kubernetes: false

docs.title: gpuprov ssh <NAME> [-- CMD...]
docs.text: Opens an interactive shell, or runs one command and propagates its exit code. It uses the recorded user and port.

docs.title: gpuprov list
docs.text:
Lists every VM row: state, provider, region and zone, type, instance id, and endpoint (host:port when the port isn't 22).

States: PROVISIONING, UP, FAILED, TERMINATED, and LEAKED. LEAKED means teardown could not be confirmed. Run down again.

docs.title: gpuprov status <NAME>
docs.text: Shows the VM row, the last operation's state (marked in flight if it was interrupted), and up to 30 recent journaled transitions with failure details. This is the place to look when a provision fails.

docs.title: gpuprov down <NAME>
docs.text: Terminates the VM's instances, waits until they are gone, deletes per-VM side resources (security group or firewall rule), and removes local SSH and kubeconfig files. Ctrl-C does not stop a teardown halfway; press it twice to force-exit, then re-run to resume.

docs.title: gpuprov kubeconfig <NAME>
docs.text: For --k8s VMs, re-runs the cluster steps (idempotent install, then API wait, kubeconfig fetch, and validation) and rewrites ~/.gpu-provisioner/kube/<NAME>.yaml.

docs.title: gpuprov tunnel <NAME>
docs.text: For clusters on clouds without inbound-port control (Prime Intellect, Docker), forwards 127.0.0.1:16443 to the node's API server. The kubeconfig of such clusters already points there. Keep it running while you use kubectl.

docs.title: Local state
docs.text:
Everything lives under ~/.gpu-provisioner, or under $GPUPROV_HOME when set:

~/.gpu-provisioner/
├── config.toml        # optional CLI config (below)
├── state.db           # SQLite: VM rows + state-machine journal
├── keys/              # the shared ed25519 keypair (generated on first use)
├── ssh/<name>         # per-VM ssh config, Include'd from ~/.ssh/config
├── sockets/           # ssh ControlMaster sockets
└── kube/<name>.yaml   # kubeconfigs of --k8s clusters (0600)

docs.title: config.toml
docs.text:
All sections are optional. Unknown keys are rejected.

[aws]
profile = "default"            # or explicit static credentials:
# access_key_id = "..."
# secret_access_key = "..."
# session_token = "..."        # optional

[gcp]
project = "my-project"         # else $GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT / gcloud config
# access_token = "..."         # else $GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN / gcloud auth print-access-token
regions = ["us-central1"]      # default failover order for --cloud gcp

[primeintellect]
api_key = "..."                # else $PRIME_API_KEY, else ~/.prime/config.json
# team_id = "..."              # bill pods to a team
# regions = ["united_states"]  # default region filter (empty = anywhere)

[docker]
# image = "my/sshd:tag"        # default: built locally from an embedded Dockerfile

[defaults]
regions = ["us-west-2", "us-east-1"]   # AWS failover order when the spec has none
disk_gb = 100
ssh_user = "ubuntu"

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
For a launch, values come from CLI flags first, then the spec YAML, then the config file. Region names are cloud-specific, so each cloud has its own default region list. AWS uses [defaults] regions; the other clouds use their own section.

Whether an empty region list is allowed is the cloud's call. AWS and GCP require at least one region. Prime Intellect treats an empty list as "anywhere in the marketplace".

docs.title: Credentials by cloud
docs.text: Cloud Resolution order AWS static keys in [aws], then [aws] profile, then the default AWS chain (env vars, ~/.aws, IMDS) GCP [gcp] access_token, then $GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN, then gcloud auth print-access-token (cached, refreshed before expiry). Project: [gcp] project, then $GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT/$CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT, then gcloud config get-value project Prime Intellect [primeintellect] api_key, then $PRIME_API_KEY, then the prime CLI's ~/.prime/config.json (the file SkyPilot reads) Docker the local Docker daemon (docker info must work)

docs.title: Kubernetes (k3s)
docs.text:
--k8s turns the VM into a single-node k3s cluster: real Kubernetes, managed by systemd on the node. You then deploy apps with plain kubectl. There is no custom controller; k3s itself is the reconciler.

gpuprov provision --name gpu-k8s --gpus L4:1 --cloud gcp --region us-central1 --k8s
export KUBECONFIG=~/.gpu-provisioner/kube/gpu-k8s.yaml
kubectl get nodes
kubectl apply -f examples/gpu-test.yaml    # runs nvidia-smi in a pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu
kubectl logs job/gpu-test

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
The cluster is a state machine layered on the VM launch machine:

  1. VM. The normal launch runs, with failover and compensation. On clouds that can open ports, it also opens 6443 (API), 80, and 443 (Traefik ingress).
  2. Install. The installer is pushed over SSH and run as root. It is idempotent: an already-running k3s is left alone. If nvidia-smi works, it installs nvidia-container-toolkit (unless the image already has it), makes nvidia the default containerd runtime, and applies the NVIDIA device plugin (pinned v0.19.3).
  3. API ready. It polls /readyz for up to 10 minutes.
  4. Kubeconfig. It reads /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml, renames the cluster/user/context to gpuprov-<name>, points server at the access endpoint, and writes it with mode 0600.
  5. Validate. On the node, it checks that the node is Ready, CoreDNS is ready, and, if a GPU is present, that nvidia.com/gpu is allocatable. In direct mode it also checks that the API port is reachable from your machine, which catches firewall problems that on-node checks can't see.

If a cluster step fails, the VM is kept (state Failed { vm }) so you can debug it with gpuprov ssh. Re-run the same provision command to retry, or run gpuprov down to remove it.

docs.title: Access modes
docs.text:
Mode When Kubeconfig server You run Direct the cloud can open ports (AWS, GCP) https://<public-ip>:6443 nothing SSH tunnel the cloud can't (Prime Intellect, Docker) https://127.0.0.1:16443 gpuprov tunnel <name> in another terminal

The API certificate covers both: the public host is added as a TLS SAN, and 127.0.0.1 is always included.

Direct mode exposure

In direct mode, ports 6443, 80, and 443 are open to 0.0.0.0/0. API access is gated by the client certificate inside the kubeconfig, so treat that file as a secret.

Docker cloud

Docker test containers don't run systemd, so the k3s installer cannot run there. Use the Docker cloud for VM-lifecycle testing only.
